summary: Discovery with Hypatia Analytics focused on p95 latency and throughput targets for a real-time analytics assistant. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) with constraints: p95 < 300ms on short prompts, streaming support, 50-200 concurrent users, and token/sec benchmarking for long-form generation. Action items: benchmark run, pricing, security docs, and follow-up deep-dive for VPC configuration.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining - Jordan from Redwood. We have Priya from the SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:04] Carlos Mendes (Hypatia CTO): Good, thanks. Wanted to focus this call on latency/throughput, we've had some issues hitting p95 targets in production.
[00:12] Priya Raman (Redwood SE): Great, can you give us your current baseline? p95, concurrency, model types?
[00:18] Aisha Khan (ML Eng): Sure. We're running a mixed workload. Short prompt responses for chat-like assistant and longer completions for reports. Right now p95 is around 480-520ms on our best path, concurrency ~60 across load balancer, but critical user-paths need p95 < 300ms.
[00:34] Liam O'Neill (DevOps): We have autoscaling but it's slow for bursts. We also stream but see token emission delays during high concurrency.
[00:42] Jordan: Okay, that makes sense. Are you currently hosted on cloud-managed endpoints or self-hosted?
[00:47] Carlos: We're mostly self-hosting on mps/gpu clusters but evaluating managed options for consistency. Security is also a requirement - need VPC or private deployment for some customers.
[00:56] Priya: Perfect. For p95 < 300ms we need to understand sequence lengths, typical tokens per response, and whether streaming is used. Do your short prompts average like 20-50 tokens?
[01:05] Aisha: Yes short chat messages average 25 tokens, longer reports are 600-1,200 tokens. The p95 SLA is most important for short chat flows.
[01:13] Jordan: Understood. Two levers to hit p95 are model choice/quantization and serving config - batching and prefix/KV cache. For short prompts we can leverage prefix caching and smaller models or distilled variants. Are you open to using a slightly smaller model for low-latency paths?
[01:25] Carlos: Potentially, but we need parity on quality for the top N intents. We also want streaming - clients expect immediate token emission.
[01:31] Priya: Streaming mainly affects tail latency because you can start sending tokens before full generation. But you still need per-token generation speed. Aiming for tokens/sec of 1000-2000 on optimized kernels is reasonable for gen models at shorter sequences.
[01:44] Liam: When you say tokens/sec, is that per GPU or per replica? We have a budget and want to estimate node counts.
[01:49] Priya: Good question - usually tokens/sec benchmarks are per-GPU for steady-state generation. Throughput for concurrent requests depends on batching and effective concurrency. For example, if one GPU can sustain 1k tokens/sec for these model sizes, and you have average response size 25 tokens, you could serve ~40 requests/sec with minimal batching. But concurrency and burst behavior change that math.
[02:10] Jordan: Also important is KV cache reuse for chat: if sessions reuse prefix tokens, the per-turn compute is lower and tokens/sec chart improves significantly.
[02:18] Carlos: Our chat sessions reuse context but not always cleanly, sigh.
[02:21] Aisha: We also saw 200-300ms jitter during peaks.
[02:26] Priya: That's likely queuing at the router or autoscaler. For Dedicated we offer reserved pools to reduce tail queuing, and we can configure burst capacity. For Private/VPC you get similar controls but you'll manage autoscaling unless we provide managed option.
[02:39] Liam: If we go Dedicated, what's the latency difference vs Hosted?
[02:43] Priya: Typically Hosted can be faster to start because we manage placement and multi-tenant optimizations, but Dedicated gives you predictability and isolation. If you reserve enough GPUs to meet peak concurrency, Dedicated p95 will be lower and more consistent. We also do kernel tuning per model to reduce p95. But Dedicated requires commit to capacity; we provide burst options to handle spikes.
[02:58] Jordan: Let me give an example: for a 13B-sized open model quantized to 4-bit, optimized kernels and continuous batching, we've seen p95 ~180-260ms on RTX/GPU class at short sequences. At longer sequences p95 grows linearly.
[03:12] Carlos: That's helpful. Can you talk about how you measure p95 - is it end-to-end including network?
[03:16] Priya: Our p95 is measured server-side from request receipt to last token emitted. End-to-end includes client network; we can provide synthetic benchmarks from our regions to estimate E2E. We'll attach benchmarking spreadsheet.
[03:28] Aisha: We need to run our prompt set through your bench.
[03:32] Priya: Absolutely. Best practice is to provide a sample prompt set and expected concurrent sessions. We can then run token/sec and p95 benchmarks in both Hosted and Dedicated thin-provision modes.
[03:41] Liam: About streaming: how does batching interact with streaming? My fear is that batching increases latency.
[03:46] Priya: Batching trades latency for throughput. For strict p95 constraints you often use small batch sizes or enable micro-batching with short time windows. Streaming still works - we can emit partial tokens from the model as soon as they are available. There's a configuration to prioritize latency (small batch, no wait) vs cost (larger batch).
[03:59] Jordan: Also caching can reduce batch needs; if a high percent of sessions have identical prefixes, batching is less necessary because results are cached.
[04:06] Carlos: For our analytics assistant many prompts share similar prefixes, so KV cache could be big win. How do you do prefix caching?
[04:12] Priya: We support prefix/KV cache at serving layer - we keep activations for common prefixes and reuse them for subsequent turns. This reduces compute by skipping early layers for a lot of tokens. It requires session affinity or a centralized cache layer. For Dedicated we can give you an architecture that colocates cache near GPUs for low latency.
[04:28] Aisha: If we were to do a pilot, what's the typical timeline to get meaningful benchmarks?
[04:33] Jordan: For a simple benchmark with your prompt set, we can run it within 48-72 hours after we get the data and access. For VPC/private deployments it takes longer due to network setup.
[04:41] Liam: Security-wise, we need SOC2, SAML, and KMS integration. Any limitations with private networks?
[04:47] Priya: We have SOC2 reports available; SSO via SAML/Okta is supported. For KMS we integrate with customer-managed keys in Private deployments; for Hosted we support envelope encryption and rotation via our KMS integrations. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs.
[05:00] Carlos: Great. On the cost side, do you have examples of RU per token or per request for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[05:05] Jordan: Pricing varies by model and quantization. We'll share a pricing sheet, but to ballpark: dedicated reserved capacity reduces per-token cost by 20-40% at scale compared to on-demand hosted, depending on utilization and batching. We'll include headroom and burst pricing options.
[05:17] Aisha: Back to benchmarking - what's your standard tokens/sec test? Do you include sampling, top-k, etc?
[05:22] Priya: We run a couple of modes: greedy sampling steady-state, and sampling with top-k/top-p for realistic outputs. We instrument per-token latency and compute tokens/sec for model and hardware. We'll run both for your prompt set.
[05:34] Liam: For concurrency planning, do you recommend overprovisioning for p95 or using autoscale?
[05:38] Priya: For p95-sensitive paths, we recommend a small buffer (20-30%) above measured peak plus autoscale for unexpected spikes. Dedicated with reserved cores plus burst capacity is a common pattern. We can simulate spikes in the bench.
[05:50] Jordan: To summarize, we'll run a 1k token/sec target benchmark on our GPUs with your prompts, share logs and a spreadsheet, send SOC2 and pricing, and schedule a follow-up deep-dive about VPC.
[06:00] Carlos: Sounds good. For the benchmark, can Priya also include a streaming vs non-streaming run so we can see p95 differences?
[06:06] Priya: Yep, we'll do both streaming and non-streaming runs and include per-token emission traces.
[06:11] Aisha: Also include quantized vs unquantized runs if possible.
[06:14] Priya: Will do. We'll run q4-bit and fp16 where applicable.
[06:18] Liam: One more question: do you support pinned model versions and rollbacks? We need consistent outputs for evaluation.
[06:23] Jordan: Yes, you can pin model versions and roll back. We also support canary rollouts and A/B.
[06:28] Carlos: OK let's schedule the technical deep-dive for next week.
[06:31] Jordan: We'll propose times in the follow-up email.
[06:33] Marta Ruiz (Product): Quick note - our product folks will want to know about latency per language. We use multiple languages in chat, will that impact p95?
[06:41] Priya: Multilingual models can have differences but kernel performance is fairly similar; we'll call out any differences in the bench.
[06:47] Carlos: Appreciate it. Any immediate blockers from your side?
[06:50] Priya: We just need the prompt set and a representative concurrency profile. Also any security requirements for shared artifacts.
[06:56] Carlos: We'll share a sanitized prompt set and CSV with concurrency by 2025-12-04.
[06:59] Jordan: Great - action items and timeline captured, we'll send the follow-up. Thanks everyone.
[07:03] End of meeting (approx 46 min).
